title: 1970 AHSME Problem 4
statement: Let \(S\) be the set of all numbers which are the sum of the squares of three consecutive integers. Then we can say that:

answerChoices.label: A
answerChoices.text: No member of \(S\) is divisible by \(2\)

answerChoices.label: B
answerChoices.text:
No member of \(S\) is divisible by \(3\) but
some member is divisible by \(11\)

answerChoices.label: C
answerChoices.text: No member of \(S\) is divisible by \(3\) or by \(5\)

answerChoices.label: D
answerChoices.text: No member of \(S\) is divisible by \(3\) or by \(7\)

solutions.text:
The sum is \[ \begin{gathered} (n-1)^2+n^2+(n+1)^2\\ =3n^2+2. \end{gathered} \] It is always congruent to \(2\pmod3,\) so no member of \(S\) is divisible by \(3.\) On the other hand, taking \(n=5\) gives \(3(25)+2=77,\) which is divisible by \(11.\)

Therefore, the correct answer is B.
hints: Their squared sum is \(3n^2+2;\) examine it modulo \(3\) and test a residue modulo \(11\)
